## People absorb what they already half know

People take up what they already half know. Anyone recognises a new thing by what it resembles in their own work. If it resembles nothing, there is nowhere to put it.

Michael Polanyi, a philosopher of science, had the line for it: *we know more than we can tell.* Your agent runs on the part of your work you never wrote down. Your teammate has their own version, about their own work, and that is where your thing has to land.

after:
## The analysis was ready. The decision never came.

At the start of 2026 I set out to redesign a whole value stream with agents. We picked the slice that takes a company's flagship product to its millions of customers. Many teams touch it.

We built a multi-agent system for the work. About fifteen people across those teams mapped their own part and uploaded their own documents. A central agent pulled it all into one map of how the work flows today.

On the first workshop day, most of them refined that map together. People had fun, and bit by bit they learned how it works. On the second day a smaller group redesigned the flow. We left with a plausible proposal and the analysis to decide on it.

We had chosen this topic with the senior leadership before we started. By the decision meeting, the urgency had gone. New priorities had come up, and fires were burning elsewhere. The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.

The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had. Companies, even when they go agentic, work first and foremost on the human principle.

Antti Tevanlinna

[What would have to be true for them to switch?](slides/what-would-have-to-be-true.md)

## Push back on the summary

Push back where the agent's summary is wrong. *"The teammate's job wasn't vague, you just didn't see it"* / *"you pulled too much out of the skill, put the edge cases back."* The artifact: the sharpened sharing file itself, plus one line in your Module 7 next-step file naming the first move. Save the conversation. It's the bridge to when work resumes.
a:
## Debrief

Five minutes. The agent reviews the sharing deliverable and sharpens whichever sharing-artifact file you produced (a skill file, an interface description, an output schedule, a context export). The evidence is what's in your Module 7 folder: your JTBD outcome statement, the patterns you picked, the technical plan, the people plan, assumptions, and failure stories. The agent reviews, rewrites the sharing artifact in place, and reports what changed. You push back on anything that's off.

{{prompt:a101-m7-debrief-sharing-artifact}}

> **Watch for slowness.** When you push back on the rewrite, the agent should edit the section you flagged, not rewrite the whole file. The prompt above tells it to. If the agent reaches for a full rewrite anyway, push back: *"Edit just the section I named."*
b:
## Debrief

Five minutes. The agent reviews the sharing deliverable and sharpens whichever sharing-artifact file you produced (a skill file, an interface description, an output schedule, a context export). The evidence is what's in your Module 7 folder: your JTBD outcome statement, the patterns you picked, the technical plan, the people plan, assumptions, and failure stories. The agent reviews, rewrites the sharing artifact in place, and reports what changed. You push back on anything that's off.

{{prompt:a101-m7-debrief-sharing-artifact}}

> **Watch for slowness.** When you push back on the rewrite, the agent should edit the section you flagged, not rewrite the whole file. The prompt above tells it to. If the agent reaches for a full rewrite anyway, push back: *"Edit just the section I named."*

Notice what this prompt insists on: name the path, overwrite in place, quote the before-and-after for every claim. When you're sharpening something for another person to use, "what got sharpened" without the actual lines is a draft pretending to be a finished thing. The before-and-after quote is how you know the sharpening reached the file, not just the summary.

## The people plan stalls on names

The technical plan fills quickly. The people plan stalls on names.

A missing name is a finding: it marks the part of this that is not built yet, and it is the part that decides whether any of the rest gets used.

So the move stays small. One name. One person whose week this would change, who would tell you plainly if it did not.
a:
## The one piece you don't decide

Every piece so far was yours to decide. This one is not. You can hand someone the context, the skill, the output, the interface. Whether they pick it up is their decision, made for their own reasons, on a Tuesday you will not be in the room for.

The thing you would most like to hand over is the one thing that will not go. You cannot hand over what you learned getting here. You can hand over four things, and none of them is what you learned.
